domain: International Law / Nuclear Governance / Treaty Interpretation
topic_summary: Analysis of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) as a contested kernel where Article IV (inalienable right to peaceful nuclear technology) and Article VI (disarmament obligation) are read differently by weapon states versus non-weapon states, producing structurally incompatible constraint regimes.

key_entities: NPT Treaty Text (1968/1970 founding document; Articles IV and VI as contested kernel)
Nuclear Weapon States (P5: US, Russia, UK, France, China; de facto authority holders)
Non-Nuclear Weapon States (NNWS signatories; restrained parties claiming breach)
IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency; verification mechanism)
Nuclear Suppliers Group (informal cartel; export control regime)
key_tensions: Vertical proliferation (weapon state arsenal expansion) vs horizontal proliferation (new weapon state emergence)
Treaty equity (reciprocal disarmament-for-restraint bargain) vs security hierarchy (two-tier order as permanent)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The NPT's pairing of Article IV (inalienable right to peaceful nuclear technology) with Article VI (disarmament obligation pursued in good faith) as a bargained exchange
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested: weapon states ground authority in security interest and verification capacity; non-weapon states ground authority in treaty reciprocity and sovereign equality

readings.commitment: Article IV is conditional on Article III verification; Article VI is aspirational and non-justiciable; authority derives from weapon states' security interest in preventing horizontal proliferation
readings.authority_grounding: Security Council P5 position; IAEA safeguards enforcement capacity; implicit threat of sanctions/withdrawal
readings.expected_structural_delta: Two-tier order permanently stabilized; weapon state arsenals excluded from treaty enforcement; non-weapon states as perpetual restraint-bearers; Article VI timeline unenforceable

readings.commitment: Article IV and Article VI are reciprocal obligations; non-weapon state restraint is conditional on weapon state disarmament progress; breach of Article VI undermines Article IV legitimacy
readings.authority_grounding: Treaty text as bilateral contract; sovereign equality principle; NNWS diplomatic coalition (NAM bloc)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Disarmament obligation becomes enforceable; failure to disarm licenses NNWS withdrawal or Article IV expansion; weapon states as treaty-breach actors; verification reciprocity required

readings.commitment: Article VI mandates complete disarmament; Article IV is illegitimate if it perpetuates dual-use proliferation risk; authority derives from humanitarian law and weapons-prohibition treaty precedent (TPNW)
readings.authority_grounding: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017); ICRC humanitarian law doctrine; civil society/non-state actor mobilization
readings.expected_structural_delta: NPT itself delegitimized as insufficient; Article IV constrained by prohibition norm; weapon possession categorically illegal; no distinction between peaceful and military programs

axiom_contradictions.basis: Nonproliferation-primary treats weapon state arsenals as outside treaty enforcement (structural exception); grand-bargain treats disarmament failure as treaty breach nullifying NNWS obligations. No single framework can hold both weapon state exceptionalism and reciprocal conditionality simultaneously.

Nonproliferation-primary legitimizes permanent weapon state status with aspirational disarmament; abolitionist categorically prohibits possession regardless of security claims. No framework can hold both 'arsenals legitimate pending eventual disarmament' and 'all possession inherently illegal' simultaneously.

Grand-bargain preserves Article IV peaceful-use right as core treaty value; abolitionist subordinates Article IV to prohibition norm (dual-use technology as proliferation vector). No framework can simultaneously treat peaceful nuclear programs as inalienable right and as illegitimate proliferation risk.

axes.selection_reason: Dominant institutional reading; highest ε (permanent two-tier extraction); structurally entrenched via P5 veto and safeguards asymmetry

axes.selection_reason: Structural alternative to nonproliferation-primary; different authority grounding (reciprocity vs hierarchy); captures NNWS coalition position
